title: Scotus and Biel follow Durandus; the view now rejected as Pelagian
source_text: XIV. Eandem vero cum Durando sententiam amplexi sunt Scotus & Gabriel Biel. Opinantur enim cum illo, hominem, etiam peccato corruptum, posse omnia praecepta moralia, seu legis naturae, secundum substantiam operum, servare per vires suas, sine gratia, licet non in ordine ad finem supernaturalem: ut testatur Estius in secundum sententiarum, Distinctione vigesima sexta paragrapho quadragesimo propositione octava. Verum haec sententia in Schola Romana communiter hodie rejicitur. Atque Estii judicio manifestum est illam ad Pelagii haeresin spectare, & contrariam ad fidem Catholicam.
pass_a_gloss: XIV. And the same opinion with Durandus Scotus and Gabriel Biel embraced. For they think with him, that man, even corrupted by sin, can keep all the moral precepts, or of the law of nature, according to the substance of the works, by his own strength, without grace, although not in order to the supernatural end: as Estius testifies on the second of the sentences, Distinction twenty-six paragraph forty proposition eight. But this opinion is commonly rejected today in the Roman School. And by the judgement of Estius it is manifest that it tends to the heresy of Pelagius, and is contrary to the Catholic faith.
pass_b_english: Scotus and Gabriel Biel took the same view as Durandus. With him they hold that man, even corrupted by sin, can by his own strength and without grace keep all the moral precepts, the precepts of the law of nature, as to the substance of the works, though not as ordered to the supernatural end. So Estius reports on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 40, proposition 8.
But the Roman School today commonly rejects this view, and in Estius's judgement it plainly leans toward the heresy of Pelagius and is contrary to the Catholic faith.

choices.why: The scholastic distinction between doing what a precept requires and doing it in the manner that orders it to salvation; kept as the technical phrase.
